creative.body:
If your doctor put you on Ozempic and then told you to just take Miralax for the constipation, please read this before you buy another bottle.

Those 2 products are working on 2 completely different parts of your body.

And the gap between them is about 6 feet of intestine.

I know because I spent 3 months and $214 figuring that out the hard way.

I'm going to tell you what I learned, what almost happened to me before I figured it out, and what's been happening to women in the GLP-1 support groups who are 18 months out, 2 years out, 3 years out, and still not right.

Because the part nobody told me, and the part I'm telling you now, is that the longer this goes uncorrected, the harder it gets to come back from.

I've been on Wegovy since last May. Down 41 pounds. My jeans fit again. People at church started telling me how great I looked. Everything was working except one thing.

I stopped going to the bathroom.

Not slowed down. Stopped. 7 days. 9 days. Once, 11.

My doctor said take Miralax. I took Miralax. Nothing. She said take it twice a day. I took it twice a day. Still nothing.

So I added Colace. Then magnesium citrate at bedtime. Then fiber gummies in the morning because my coworker said they worked for her. Then I switched to psyllium husk because someone in a Facebook group said gummies don't have enough fiber to matter.

By October I had 5 products on my bathroom counter and I hadn't gone in 8 days.

I stood in the Walgreens laxative aisle on a Tuesday night trying to pick between Dulcolax and senna tea and I realized I had no idea why I was there. I'd already tried 4 things. None of them worked. I was just buying a 5th because I didn't know what else to do.

That was the moment it stopped being frustrating and started being something else.

I wasn't confused anymore. I was exhausted. I was spending money and swallowing pills and drinking powders and nothing was moving and nobody could tell me why.

My husband asked me one night if I'd eaten dinner and I said yes.

I hadn't.

I'd stopped eating full meals because the pressure in my stomach was unbearable by evening and I figured if I ate less, there'd be less to get stuck. I was on a weight loss medication and I was starving myself on top of it. Not to lose weight. To avoid the pain of food sitting inside me for days.

That night my granddaughter was at the house. She's 9. She came into the kitchen for water and looked at me sitting at the table not eating and she asked, "Grandma, are you sick?"

I told her no.

But I sat there after she went back upstairs and I thought about how to answer that question honestly. I wasn't sick. I had a prescription that was working. I had a body that was supposed to be celebrating. I had a granddaughter who was watching me skip dinner and lie about it.

Whatever this was, I couldn't keep doing it.

I had a follow-up with my GI nurse practitioner 2 weeks later. Routine visit. She asked how the Wegovy was going and I told her fine, except for the constipation. I listed everything I was taking. Miralax. Colace. Magnesium. Fiber. She let me finish.

Then she said something I hadn't heard from anyone.

"All of those work on your colon. Your problem isn't in your colon."

She said it in the same flat tone she'd ask me about my blood pressure. Like it should have been obvious. Like every other doctor I'd seen should have already told me.

None of them had.

I asked her what she meant.

She said GLP-1 medications slow down the stomach, and the constipation I was experiencing was a stomach problem, not a colon problem. She said I could look into it if I wanted to understand why nothing was helping.

I asked her why none of my doctors had told me this in 6 months.

She paused.

"Because most of them haven't read the gastroenterology literature on it yet. The drug came up too fast. The protocols haven't caught up. Most patients on GLP-1s who come in with constipation get sent home with another laxative."

Then she said the part that stayed with me on the drive home.

"I have a patient who waited 2 years before anyone told her this. Her stomach is permanently slowed now. The medical term is gastroparesis. We're managing it but we can't reverse it. Don't wait."

I sat in my car in the parking lot for a long time after that.

That night I sat at my kitchen table with my laptop and I searched "why do GLP-1 medications cause constipation."

Not how to fix it. Why it happens.

For the first time I wasn't looking for a product. I was looking for an explanation.

GLP-1 medications work by slowing down gastric emptying. That's the whole mechanism behind the appetite suppression. Your stomach holds food longer so you feel full longer. That's the point.

But when your stomach slows down too much, food doesn't just sit there quietly. It sits there and ferments. Bacteria break it down. Gas builds up. Your stomach distends. And the food that's supposed to move into your intestines and eventually reach your colon doesn't get there. Or it gets there so slowly that everything downstream backs up.

The constipation isn't happening in the colon. It's starting in the stomach.

And every single product I'd been taking, Miralax, Colace, Dulcolax, magnesium, fiber, works on the colon.

It was like a clogged drain. Every product I was using was clean water being poured into the top of the sink. The water just sat there. Because the clog was 3 feet down the pipe, in a place none of those products could reach.

Miralax pulls water into the colon to soften stool. But there was barely any stool in my colon to soften. The food was still sitting in my stomach. Water poured into an empty sink.

Dulcolax triggers contractions in the colon wall. But there was nothing in my colon to push. It was contracting around empty space. That's why it gave me cramps with zero results.

Fiber adds bulk. But adding bulk to a system where the stomach has already stopped moving forward just made the backup worse. The pressure got worse. The bloating got worse. And nothing came out anyway.

Magnesium citrate does the same thing as Miralax. Pulls water into the lower intestine. Same organ. Same problem. Different brand name.

I'd spent 3 months taking 4 different products that all did the same thing to the same part of my body. A part of my body that wasn't even where the problem was.

Once I understood that, the question changed.

It wasn't "which laxative should I try next." It was "what actually gets the stomach moving again."

And that's what I spent the next 3 hours reading about. Until 2 in the morning.

The first thing I found was a compound called apigenin. It's concentrated in celery. And what the research showed was that it acts as a natural prokinetic. Meaning it helps the smooth muscle of your stomach start contracting again. Not the colon. The stomach. The actual part GLP-1 medications are slowing down.

That was the unclog. Something that worked where the problem was.

But while food is sitting in the stomach fermenting, gas builds up. Sulfur compounds. That's the bloating, the distension, the feeling like you're inflated by dinner. Apigenin doesn't do anything for the gas already trapped from weeks of slowdown.

The second piece I found was chlorophyllin. It binds to those sulfur compounds and breaks them down. Deals with the gas that's been building up because the stomach hasn't been emptying.

2 pieces. Then I needed something for the third part. Once the stomach is moving again and the gas is handled, food finally moves downstream into a gut that's been mostly empty for weeks. The bacteria there are weak. They need something to come back online. A prebiotic fiber. But not the bulk-adding kind. The kind that feeds the good bacteria in the lower gut so that when food finally does move through, the rest of the system is ready for it.

I went back to my bathroom and looked at every product on the counter.

Miralax. Nothing for the stomach. Colace. Nothing for the stomach. The fiber I'd been choking down. Bulk-adding, not feeding. Nothing for the gas.

Not one of those products did the first 2 things. Not one of them did the third correctly either.

The list I needed: standardized apigenin to wake the stomach back up. Chlorophyllin for the sulfur gas. A low-dose prebiotic that fed bacteria instead of bulking up the pipe.

I had a checklist for the first time in 6 months.

I went on Amazon that night and ordered the celery capsule with the most reviews. 4.6 stars. Twelve thousand reviews. $19. Prime shipping.

3 weeks later the bloating was worse, not better, and I'd had no movement in 8 days. I called the company. The woman on the phone read me the label. Celery powder, 500 milligrams per capsule. No standardized apigenin content listed. I asked her how much actual apigenin was in 500 milligrams of celery powder. She didn't know.

I went back to the research. The studies on apigenin used standardized extract at 30 to 50 milligrams of pure apigenin daily. I'd been taking maybe 1 or 2.

I'd had the right ingredient at the wrong dose, in a form my body couldn't absorb.

Another month, another bottle, no closer to a working stomach.

The next day at my granddaughter's soccer game I ended up next to another mom from our neighborhood. Older woman. We'd talked a few times. I knew she was a pharmacist somewhere local.

I don't know why but I told her. About the Wegovy. About the laxatives. About the celery capsules that turned out to be glorified vegetable powder.

She listened the whole way through. Then she said, "Most of those celery products are filler. I tested them."

That was it. That was the whole sentence.

Then her son got knocked over on the field and she ran out to him and the conversation ended.

She texted me 2 days later. Said if I wanted to talk more about the testing she'd be at the pharmacy that afternoon.

I went.

She told me her older sister had gastroparesis from years on Reglan and never got it fully back. After her sister died, she'd asked a colleague at her pharmacy to run third-party assays on 22 of the most popular celery and apigenin supplements on the market.

18 of them tested under 5 milligrams of standardized apigenin per serving. 5 had heavy metal contamination above safe limits. 3 had no detectable apigenin at all. Just rice powder and gelatin.

Only 2 products consistently tested at clinical-grade apigenin concentration.

She told me one of them was a small company called Motilli. They made a celery juice fiber gummy specifically formulated for women on GLP-1 medications. Standardized apigenin extract, not powder. Combined with chlorophyllin for the sulfur gas and a low-dose prebiotic for the downstream support.

Her own daughter was on Mounjaro. Had been on Motilli for 4 months. Down 40 pounds, no constipation, no bloating, eating normal dinners again.

"She's the reason I tested everything else. I needed to know there was nothing better. There isn't."

She wrote the name down on a prescription pad and handed it to me.

I pulled up Motilli on my phone before I even started the car.

Standardized apigenin extract on the label. Not powder. Not ground celery. The actual extract at the actual dose the studies used.

Chlorophyllin listed second.

A low-dose prebiotic listed third.

It was the first product I'd looked at since October that had all 3 things on the list I'd built at my kitchen table. Apigenin to restart the stomach. Chlorophyllin for the sulfur gas. A prebiotic that fed bacteria instead of bulking up the pipe.

I ordered a bottle that night.

The first 4 days, nothing.

Day 5, I noticed the bloating was less intense by evening. Not gone. Less. I didn't think much of it.

Day 7, my husband mentioned at dinner that I looked less puffy. He said my face looked "normal again." I didn't know what to do with that.

Day 9, I went. On my own. No laxative. No magnesium the night before. I just woke up and went.

I sat there for a second afterward because I honestly couldn't remember the last time that had happened without me forcing it.

Day 14, I ate a full plate of pasta with my husband and his brother who was visiting from Tucson. 3 hours later I was on the couch laughing at a movie and I realized I hadn't thought about my stomach once.

Week 3, my granddaughter was over again on a Saturday. We made cookies. I ate two. We sat at the kitchen table and she told me about her teacher and I drank coffee like a person who didn't have to plan her day around what her body might or might not do.

She didn't ask me if I was sick this time.

By week 4 it was consistent. Most mornings. No cramping. No emergency. No tracking.

By week 6 I was sleeping through the night without that low pressure I'd gotten used to under my ribs every evening. I'd stopped noticing it. Until it was gone, and then I noticed the absence.

I had my follow-up with the GI nurse practitioner in March.

She asked how the constipation was.

I told her gone. Daily. No laxatives, no magnesium, no fiber. I told her about the apigenin and the chlorophyllin and the prebiotic. About the company. About the pharmacist.

She typed something into her chart. Then she looked up.

"Whatever you're doing, keep doing it. Your stomach is moving again. That's what we wanted."

She didn't smile. She just nodded. Like someone who'd seen enough women not get this answer.

I walked out and sat in my car for a minute, the same parking lot where I'd cried 4 months earlier, and I let myself believe it was actually over.

I walked past the laxative aisle at Walgreens last week. Didn't stop. Didn't even slow down.

That aisle owned me for 3 months. Every Tuesday or Wednesday I'd be standing there reading boxes trying to figure out which one would be the one that finally worked.

They all worked. They all did exactly what they were supposed to do.

They just did it to the wrong organ.

I'm a 54-year-old woman who spent $214 and 3 months on products that couldn't have helped me because they weren't designed for the problem I actually had.

And I spent another month and another bottle on the right ingredient at the wrong dose, which is the exact trap I want you to avoid.

If you're on a GLP-1 and you're rotating through laxatives and none of them are doing anything, it's not the products. It's not you. It's that the problem is in your stomach and everything you're taking works on your colon.

And if you've already figured that out and you're now reaching for a celery powder capsule from Amazon, please pause for a second. Standardized apigenin extract is not the same thing as ground-up celery in a pill. The clinical research is on the extract, at the dose. Anything less is another month you don't get back.

The link is below if you want it.

A few notes on what to expect.

They run a 90-day money-back guarantee on it, which is the only reason I tried it after I'd been burned twice already. Anyone who has been told for 6 months to add another laxative while their body refuses to work deserves to find out for themselves without losing anything else.

They batch-produce in small quantities because apigenin degrades when it's exposed to light and heat for too long. The bottles sell out for stretches when more women in the GLP-1 groups find them. If you go to the link and the bottle is in stock, I would not wait until next week.

I'm not going to promise you what I can't.

I'm going to tell you what happened to me. I went from 8-day stretches and skipped dinners and a granddaughter asking if I was sick, to making cookies on a Saturday morning and not noticing my stomach.

That took 6 weeks.

If you've already given 6 months to the wrong aisle, 6 weeks on the right one is the trade I would make every time.

The link is below.

P.S. The pharmacist's daughter was on Mounjaro for 4 months before her mom found Motilli. Mine took 6 weeks to bring me back. If your daughter or your mother or your sister is on a GLP-1 right now and quietly skipping dinner, please send her the link. She might not tell you what's happening. I didn't tell my husband for 8 weeks.

P.P.S. The patient my GI nurse practitioner mentioned, the one who waited 2 years, has gastroparesis now. They're managing it with a feeding regimen and motility drugs. She can't reverse it. She told her doctor that she didn't realize the constipation was connected to the medication. That she thought it was age, or stress, or something she'd done. She'd been on Ozempic for 21 months when she finally went in. The longer your stomach stays slowed, the harder it gets to come back. That's what the nurse practitioner told me in October, and I didn't fully understand it until I saw what 6 weeks of the right thing could do. I'm not trying to scare you. I'm telling you the same thing she told me. Don't wait.
creative.title: I spent $214 on four different laxatives and they all did the same thing to the same organ
